children: Southwest Airlines is jumping into the airport lounge fray.

The airline will open swanky lounges in Austin, Texas; Baltimore; Nashville, Tenn.; and Honolulu, hoping to lure fliers to a new high-end credit card it plans to launch next year. JPMorgan Chase is partnering with Southwest on the lounges and will issue the new card.
Construction is under way, with plans to open the first of the enclaves in late 2027. Eventually the Dallas-based airline is planning a network of at least 11 lounges.

The lounges will primarily be available to travelers with the new Southwest premium credit card. The airline hasn't yet said what the annual fee for the card will be, but other high-end airline and travel cards can cost hundreds of dollars a year.

"We definitely believe that from a competitive standpoint, this makes us even more competitive because it's been a request from our customer base for so long," Southwest Chief Executive Bob Jordan said.
Southwest is the biggest carrier of domestic passengers, but it is coming late to the lounge game. Exclusive spaces didn't fit with the airline's egalitarian ethos.

But that is changing, and lately the company's lounge ambitions have been one of the worst-kept secrets in aviation. Executives have teased plans for months. Local media and industry publications have tracked Southwest's moves as it snapped up space at airports around the country.

The airline believes it can match-or exceed-the level of luxury its rivals offer, with signature bars and chef-inspired meals. JPMorgan brings expertise from its own network of upscale Chase Sapphire airport lounges, and Southwest executives said the experience in its lounges will be comparable, with some Southwest flair.
"It will be more elevated than what they're traditionally used to seeing from Southwest. That's actually our strategy here," said Tony Roach, Southwest's chief customer and brand officer.

Once a budget pioneer that stripped out frills and offered only one type of seating, Southwest has been trying to bring in more revenue by matching some practices of other airlines and catering to customers' appetite for premium travel experiences.

Over the past few years, Southwest ditched hallmark features like open seating and started charging for checked bags. And it has added rows of extra-legroom seating to its planes in an effort to win over fliers willing to shell out for added comforts.

The desire to escape the airport terminal in an exclusive oasis has been an enduring travel trend. Lounges have helped persuade travelers to stay within an airline's loyalty program and to sign up for credit cards that carry hefty fees.

Airlines and credit-card companies have gone on a lounge building spree in an effort to keep up with demand and to prevent long lines and crowding, kitting out more opulent spaces in an amenities arms race. Southwest isn't the only carrier that decided it can no longer afford to sit out the building boom: JetBlue Airways opened up two new lounges in the past year.

Southwest executives spent months visiting lounges to figure out what works and how to avoid potential pitfalls. They want to wow customers with their decor, high-end finishes, and impressive food and drinks.
Their biggest takeaway: size matters. The first four lounges will range from 13,000 square feet in Honolulu to roughly 30,000 square feet in Nashville and Baltimore.

The airline hasn't ruled out offering memberships and could sell day passes, but is trying to avoid letting too many people in and then having to pull back if spaces become too packed, as some lounge operators have had to do.
"We know customers want access to a premium lounge network, but we also know they hate overcrowding and they hate having to wait," Jordan said.
